title: John Hammond and the Bessie Smith chapter that never came
summary: Hammond was to write the Bessie Smith chapter, the TV special on his life, and the afternoon Russell spent in his Columbia office.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band

blocks.x: Yeah, I don't know. Anyway, I started to laugh about that. So naturally, we weren't putting him in the New Orleans chapter, but he deserved to be in the book and all, too. I mean, a lot of people left out of the book. It just happened to be an anthology that they took a few people and tried to get them to write about their favorites. Incidentally, there should have been a chapter on Bessie Smith, too, which John Hammond had promised to write.

No, I remember going to see John Hammond one afternoon. I thought about it. They had this big, you might say, TV spectacular, you know, the big special on the two weeks. Did you all see that? About two months ago.
No, John Hammond. Oh, yeah. His whole life. I thought that was that. I thought part of it. Yeah, which is quite good.

He had a lot of the musicians that he'd known. There aren't so many of them left. He didn't have Basie on for some reason, but some of his musicians. And a few of the blues things, unfortunately, they had his son on, too, who's a good guy, no doubt. But they had him on right after Sonny Terry, playing guitar and harmonica, which he should have. Actually, the young John Hammond likes Sonny Terry. He did a duet with him. As soon as it was over, he began applauding. I mean, he didn't try to steal the show. I mean, he knows that he's not in that class, but commercially, certainly, would outsell any of the Sonny Terry, I guess, stuff now. But anyway, I thought about that. The time I went to see Hammond, he was at Columbia Records then, and I spent almost the whole afternoon there. He'd be talking on the phone all the time, and as soon as he'd hang up the phone, it would ring again. I remember one musician, some guy in Harlem, called him up. Some woman was suing him as the father of her child or something. So John had to get him a lawyer. I mean, he would do everything he could for all the musicians. Finally, at about six o'clock, Benny Goodman called him up, and so he grabbed his hand. So, sorry, I've got to go to dinner. He had to go to dinner with Benny. Let's see. Benny married his sister, did he?

Something like that. John didn't marry Benny Goodman's sister, no. I think it was the other way around. Well, anyway, Hammond was supposed to write the Bessie Smith chapter. I remember once I did get a few questions in. He said, well, sometime we'll get together, and he would dictate it, and I was supposed to write it down. And I was just there. I had no intention of working with him on anything.

The Bessie Smith chapter. And then after, he sort of defaulted on it. Not because of the bad intentions. He really intended to try to do it, but he was just doing too many things. As I say, when he talked all afternoon there and could hardly get in a word. I remember on the way out, then I was collecting money for Bunk's teeth at that time, too. Ramsey and I were trying to get money together to have Dr. Bessie get a set of false teeth for Bunk. And Hammond made some remark. Of course, Bunk will never play again, but he was still glad to give. He gave $10. That was a big donation, bigger than hardly anybody gave more than a dollar or two. But he said, oh, no, we'll never hear Bunk. I said, maybe we'll get to hear him. He'll never play again, but he was glad to help out. So anyway, he's a very nice guy and always has been. But anyway, that explains, so I'm not trying to criticize him for not having time to write up to Bessie, because I'm sure he was certainly the number one Bessie Smith fan, you might say, of almost all time. At least he recorded him. He made those last four sides.
